title: Equivalent Expressions, Part 1: The Idea and an Easy Problem

beats.say: Two expressions are equivalent if they give the same value for every allowed x. They may look different, but they describe exactly the same quantity.
This skill is about rewriting. You expand products, factor polynomials, simplify with exponent rules, and reshape fractions that contain polynomials.
Most questions show one expression and ask which answer choice equals it, or ask for a constant that makes two forms match.
Expanding means multiplying every term in one factor by every term in the other, and then combining like terms.
beats.item: Expand: every term times every term

beats.say: Factoring is expanding in reverse. For a x squared plus b x plus c, find two numbers that multiply to a times c and add to b, and then split the middle term.
If two polynomials are equal for all x, their matching coefficients are equal. This lets you solve for unknown constants.
beats.item: Equal for all x: match coefficients

beats.say: Radicals are fractional exponents. The n-th root of x to the m equals x to the m over n. Convert first, then use the exponent rules.
To simplify a fraction of polynomials, factor the top and the bottom, and cancel common factors. Never cancel individual terms.
Here are the four exponent rules you need. When you multiply powers with the same base, you add the exponents. So x squared times x to the fifth is x to the seventh.
When you divide powers with the same base, you subtract the exponents. So x to the sixth divided by x squared is x to the fourth.
When you raise a power to a power, you multiply the exponents, and the coefficient is raised to that power too. So three x squared, cubed, is twenty-seven x to the sixth.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal. So x to the negative two is one over x squared.
Three special products appear again and again. A plus b, squared, equals a squared plus two a b plus b squared. The middle term is easy to forget.
A minus b, squared, equals a squared minus two a b plus b squared. And a squared minus b squared factors as a plus b times a minus b.
Easy example. Write two x minus three, times four x plus one, minus five x, in the form a x squared plus b x plus c. We expand first, and then combine like terms.
Multiply every term in the first factor by every term in the second. That gives four products. Then we keep the minus five x at the end.
Two x times four x is eight x squared. Two x times one is two x. Negative three times four x is negative twelve x. Negative three times one is negative three.
Now combine the x terms. Two x minus twelve x minus five x is negative fifteen x. The x squared term and the constant stay the same.
Check with x equal to one. The original is negative one times five, minus five, which is negative ten. The answer is eight minus fifteen minus three, which is also negative ten.
To recap. Equivalent expressions have the same value for every x. Expand by multiplying every term by every term.
beats.item: Expand every term by every term

beats.say: Use the exponent rules: add when multiplying, subtract when dividing, multiply when raising a power to a power.
